newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak crown avoids Czech fate, but seen weakening.
newsitem.headline: Slovak crown avoids Czech fate, but seen weakening.

text.p: The Slovak crown can avoid the kind of speculative assault suffered in the neighbouring Czech Republic, but its ballooning trade deficit will force a moderate depreciation in the longer term, dealers said on Wednesday.

The Slovak National Bank (NBS) fixed the crown on Wednesday at 33.6 to the dollar and 19.4 to the mark implying a deviation of minus 0.67 percent against its mark/dollar basket, unchanged from Tuesday.
The Czech crown was trading on Wednesday at around nine percent below the mid-point of its former basket.

Despite widespread predictions that the Slovak crown would be forced to follow the Czech central bank which gave in to massive pressure and allowed its currency to float last week, the NBS has successfully squeezed crown liquidity, keeping foreign speculators at bay.
"The NBS seems to be winning the battle with London at the moment...there is no liquidity in the Slovak crown," said Tibor Fratrik of ING Bank.
Although the NBS has been sporadically adding small amounts of liquidity, the interbank market remains around 38 percent short of required funds to meet minimum reserve requirements.
The central bank policy of keeping the market short is designed to prevent speculators from borrowing crowns on long positions to sell on spot.
"It would be extremely expensive for anyone to go short on Slovak crown positions...the NBS does not want to budge on this," said one dealer at a foreign bank based in Bratislava.

The policy of squeezing liquidity on the interbank market mirrors the Czech National Bank's failed strategy in defending the Czech crown but the dealer, who asked not to be named, said the two situations were not analagous.

"First of all, I would say in the Slovak market it is much more a squaring of positions although there is an element of speculation. In the Czech Republic it was an outright attack on the currency," he said.

The fall of the Czech crown was fuelled by pressure from London-based institutions who said the pre-crisis levels of the Czech crown were unsustainable because of the country's huge and growing trade deficit.
One London-based dealer for an international banking house, who also requested anonymity, said the trade situation would ultimately decide the fate of the Slovak crown as well.
"It seems a little ridiculous to have such a disparity between the Slovak and Czech crowns. So much of their trade is together that the Slovaks are going to have problems," he said.
"In any case the Slovak trade deficit with the rest of the world is just too high," he said.
Slovakia is already running a near two billion crown trade deficit with the Czech Republic, which accounts for around a quarter of its total trade turnover.
Slovakia's overall trade deficit in the first four months of the year rose to 28 billion crowns from 21 billion in the same period in 1996.

Dealers polled by Reuters on Wednesday said they did not expect the Slovak crown to depreciate even in the longer term by anything like levels seen in Prague and they thought the NBS would be able to hold the currency within the current plus/minus seven percent bands.
The most pessimistic prediction put the crown at minus five percent against the basket by the end of the year.
